Causal-Paced Deep Reinforcement Learning

Geonwoo Cho  Jaegyun Im Doyoon Kim  Sundong Kim

[ gwcho.public, jaegyun.public, dykim.research]@gmail.com, sundong@gist.ac.kr

Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology

Abstract

Designing effective task sequences is crucial for curriculum reinforcement learning (CRL), where agents must gradually acquire skills by training on intermediate tasks. A key challenge in CRL is to identify tasks that promote exploration, yet are similar enough to support effective transfer. While recent approach suggests comparing tasks via their Structural Causal Models (SCMs), the method requires access to ground-truth causal structures, an unrealistic assumption in most RL settings. In this work, we propose Causal-Paced Deep Reinforcement Learning (CP-DRL), a curriculum learning framework aware of SCM differences between tasks based on interaction data approximation. This signal captures task novelty, which we combine with the agent's learnability, measured by reward gain, to form a unified objective. Empirically, CP-DRL outperforms existing curriculum methods on the Point Mass benchmark, achieving faster convergence and higher returns. CP-DRL demonstrates reduced variance with comparable final returns in the Bipedal Walker-Trivial setting, and achieves the highest average performance in the Infeasible variant. These results indicate that leveraging causal relationships between tasks can improve the structure-awareness and sample efficiency of curriculum reinforcement learning. We provide the full implementation of CP-DRL to facilitate the reproduction of our main results at https://github.com/Cho-Geonwoc/CP-DRL.

1   Introduction

Just as a child first learns to crawl before walking and running, intelligent behavior in complex environments is rarely acquired in a single leap. Instead, learning unfolds through a gradual accumulation of simpler skills that scaffold more advanced capabilities. This principle underlies the idea of curriculum learning in reinforcement learning (RL), where agents are trained on a structured sequence of tasks that progressively increase in complexity (Narvekar et al., 2020; Florensa et al., 2018; Klink et al., 2022). By mastering simpler subtasks before facing the target task, the agent can avoid inefficient exploration and accelerate learning.

A core challenge in curriculum reinforcement learning (CRL) is to measure how tasks differ, identify what the agent has not yet learned, and expose it to novel yet transferable tasks (Hughes et al., 2024). Existing approaches typically approximate task differences using agent-centric signals, such as regret (Jiang et al., 2021) or value disagreement (Zhang et al., 2020), but these are inherently policy-dependent and sensitive to noise. As a more principled alternative, Li et al. (2024) propose comparing tasks via differences in their Structural Causal Models (SCMs), enabling a policy-independent and structure-aware measure of transferability.

While SCM-based comparison provides a principled way to quantify task differences, it relies on access to the true causal structure, which is rarely available in realistic RL environments (Zanga et al., 2022). In this work, we propose Causal-Paced Deep Reinforcement Learning (CP-DRL), a

### 2.2 Structural Causal Model in RL

A Structural Causal Model (SCM) describes causal relationships between variables (Pearl, 2009; Pearl & Bareinboim, 2011). An SCM \( \mathcal{M} \) is defined as a tuple (U, V, \( \mathcal{F}, P) \), where U is a set of exogenous (unobserved) variables, V is a set of endogenous (observed) variables, \( \mathcal{F} = \{f_V : Pa(V) \cup U_V \rightarrow V\}_{V \in V} \) is a set of structural functions, where each \( f_V \) determines \( V \) based on its endogenous parents \( Pa(V) \subseteq V \) (endogenous variables that directly influence \( V \)) and exogenous inputs \( U_V \subseteq U \) (exogenous variables that directly influence \( V \)), and \( P(U) \) is the distribution over \( U \), from which the exogenous variables are sampled.

From an RL perspective, MDP can be interpreted through the lens of SCM, where the state space S, the action space X, and the reward space Y are subsets of the set of endogenous variables V, and the randomness in the reward and transition functions is captured by the set of exogenous variables U (Li et al., 2024). In this paper, we assume a deterministic setting without exogenous variables, i.e., there is no underlying randomness in the environment. The resulting causal structure is illustrated in Figure 2. Here, \( s_t, s_{t+1} \in S \), \( a_t, a_{t+1} \in X \), and \( r_t, r_{t+1} \in Y \), and the structural functions in \( \mathcal{F} \) map \( (s_t, a_t) \) to both \( s_{t+1} \) and \( r_t \).

### 2.3 Curriculum reinforcement learning via constrained optimal transport

Our method is built upon CURROT (Klink et al., 2022), which makes a curriculum using the optimal transport problem with constraints.

\[
p_W(c) = \arg \min_p \mathcal{W}_2(p(c), \mu(c)) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad 
\begin{cases} 
p(c) > 0 \Rightarrow \mathcal{J}(\pi, c) \geq \delta \quad \forall c \in \mathcal{C} \\
\mathcal{W}_2(p(c), q(c)) \leq \epsilon 
\end{cases} 
\] (2)

It tries to minimize the 2-Wasserstein distance \( \mathcal{W}_2 \), the distance between the current source task distribution \( p(c) \) and the target task distribution \( \mu(c) \), with two constraints: (1) among all tasks, only those with nonzero probability under \( p(c) \)-i.e., tasks actually selected for training-must yield an expected return above a threshold \( \delta \) (which decreases over time), and (2) the Wasserstein distance between consecutive source task distributions \( p(c) \) and \( q(c) \) should be lower than the threshold \( \epsilon \). This optimization enables the construction of a curriculum that smoothly approaches the target distribution, while maintaining per-task expected return \( \mathcal{J}(\pi, c) \) above a decreasing threshold \( \delta \) and bounding the distributional shift between successive task distributions.

### 3 Method

We propose a curriculum learning method that encourages the agent to explore tasks with underexplored causal structures. To achieve this, we introduce the Causal Misalignment (CM) score, which quantifies how unfamiliar a task's causal structure is relative to the agent's previously learned experience. We empirically analyze the relationship between the CM score and underlying causal differences in the CausalWorld environment (Ahmed et al., 2021). We incorporate this score into CURROT to iteratively update the task distribution. By guiding the agent toward tasks with high causal misalignment, our method promotes more efficient exploration and fosters generalizable learning.

3.1 Prioritizing Causally underexplored Tasks in Curriculum Learning

To construct an effective curriculum, it is essential to accurately quantify how a new task differs from previously encountered ones in terms of learning dynamics and structural complexity (Hughes et al., 2024). If the SCMs of tasks were available, they could serve as a principled basis for comparing tasks in terms of their underlying causal mechanisms (Li et al., 2024). However, direct access to SCMs is rarely feasible in realistic reinforcement learning environments, and uncovering such structures from purely observational data remains a challenging problem (Zanga et al., 2022; Zeng et al., 2024). In deterministic settings, the interplay among state, action, transition, and reward defines a structured dependency that implicitly captures the task’s causal structure. Thus, the causal difference between two tasks can be approximated by aggregating the differences in these four components. To estimate each component-wise difference, we train dedicated models using trajectories collected from previously experienced tasks and compute disagreement among ensemble predictions.

State encoder: $z_t^s \sim q_{\phi_s}(z_t^s \mid s_t)$
State decoder: $\hat{s}_t \sim p_{\theta_s}(\hat{s}_t \mid z_t^s)$
Action encoder: $z_t^a \sim q_{\phi_a}(z_t^a \mid a_t)$
Action decoder: $\hat{a}_t \sim p_{\theta_a}(\hat{a}_t \mid z_t^a)$
Transition predictor: $\hat{s}_{t+1} \sim p_{\phi_{\tau}}(\hat{s}_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)$
Reward predictor: $\hat{r}_t \sim p_{\phi_r}(\hat{r}_t \mid s_t, a_t)$

We train six separate neural networks. $(i, \hat{a}, \hat{s}_{t+1}, \hat{r}_t)$ denote the model’s reconstruction or prediction of a corresponding variable. The state encoder $q_{\phi_s}(z_t^s \mid s_t)$ and the state decoder $p_{\theta_s}(\hat{s}_t \mid z_t^s)$ encode the current state $s_t$ into a latent representation $z_t^s$ and reconstruct it to the state $\hat{s}_t$. The action encoder $q_{\phi_a}(z_t^a \mid a_t)$ and the action decoder $p_{\theta_a}(\hat{a}_t \mid z_t^a)$ encode the action $a_t$ into a latent representation $z_t^a$ and reconstruct it to the action $\hat{a}_t$. The transition predictor $p_{\phi_{\tau}}(\hat{s}_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)$ predicts the next state based on the current state and action, approximating the environment’s transition function. The reward predictor $p_{\phi_r}(\hat{r}_t \mid s_t, a_t)$ predicts rewards for the current state and action, modeling the environment’s reward function. The detailed architecture of these neural networks is provided in Appendix B.3.

$\mathcal{L}_{\text{state}} = \|\hat{s}_t - s_t\|_2^2 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{KL}(q_{\phi_s}(z_t^s \mid s_t) \mid \mathcal{N}(0, I))$
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{action}} = \|\hat{a}_t - a_t\|_2^2 + \beta_2 \cdot \text{KL}(q_{\phi_a}(z_t^a \mid a_t) \mid \mathcal{N}(0, I))$
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{transition}} = \|\hat{s}_{t+1} - s_{t+1}\|_2^2$
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{reward}} = \|\hat{r}_t - r_t\|_2^2$

These models are trained using separate loss functions, each guiding a distinct component of the causal structure. The state and action losses, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{state}}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\text{action}}$, guide the model to accurately reconstruct the state and action, respectively, ensuring that the latent representations capture sufficient information to regenerate the original inputs. These losses also regularize the latent distributions toward a standard Gaussian prior via KL divergence as in Higgins et al. (2017). The transition loss, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{transition}}$, guides the model to approximate the transition dynamics by predicting the next state given the current state and action. Similarly, the reward loss, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{reward}}$, promotes accurate modeling of the reward function by supervising reward prediction from the current state and action.

While component-wise neural networks enable the separate modeling of individual environment components, simply training these models is insufficient to assess the causal difference between a new task and previously learned tasks. To quantify this difference, we train an ensemble of K networks for each of the four components-state, action, transition, and reward-and measure the structural unawareness of each component through ensemble disagreement, computed as the standard deviation of predictions across ensemble members as in Zhang et al. (2020).

Disagreement: $i = \text{std}\left(\left\{\hat{y}_i^{(k)}(\cdot)\right\}_{k=1}^K\right), \quad i \in \{\text{state, action, transition, reward}\}$

Figure 4: Disagreement metrics across tasks T1–T4. Each metric is computed after training on T1 for X 10 episodes and sampling 5 episodes from each task. Transition, state, and action disagreements increase monotonically, suggesting they effectively reflect causal differences. Reward disagreement shows no clear trend due to reward sparsity and random trajectory collection.

Figure 3 presents the averaged disagreement metrics over three random seeds. Transition, state, and action disagreements increase monotonically from T1 to T4, aligning well with the intended causal differences induced by task variations. In contrast, reward disagreement shows no consistent trend, likely due to sparse reward signals and the use of random policies during data collection. These results validate that the proposed component-wise disagreement metrics-especially for state, action, and transition-serve as effective proxies for capturing structural differences across tasks.

Moreover, further analysis in Appendix E reveals that transition disagreement is primarily influenced by both block size and action magnitude, action disagreement correlates with action scale, and state disagreement increases with block size. These findings reinforce our interpretation that modular disagreement meaningfully reflects the causal components underlying task variations.

## 4 Experiments

We evaluated our method, CP-DRL, on two benchmark environments: Point Mass (PM) and Bipedal Walker (BW). For the PM environment, we used Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) as the student algorithm, while for BW, we employed Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) as in Klink et al. (2022). Visualizations of each environment are provided in Figure 5.

For comparison, we evaluated several curriculum learning baselines, including CURROT, SPRL, GoalGAN, ALPGMM, ACL, PLR, and VDS (Klink et al., 2022; 2021a; Florensa et al., 2018; Portelas et al., 2020; Graves et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020). All experiments are conducted with multiple random seeds to ensure statistical reliability, 10 seeds for PM, 5 seeds for BW trivi

and the transition between experts and non-experts.1. **Hierarchical Organization**: 
   - Policies/Key Components: Trait \(\text{SAC}\) and reward learning are split into separate objectives.
   - Predictive Power: The two objectives of SAC and \(\text{Reward}\) play crucial roles in learning a policy that matches the rewards.

2. **State Predictions**:
   - State prediction is derived from a top-down, reward-free model which is trained on high-level features.
   - The input to this model is a set of latent variables \(w\).

3. **Latent Word Predictions**:
   - Each latent word is connected to a probability distribution over candidate words for that word.
   - For each word \(w\), a distribution \[p(\postcode_texttext, \pretexttexttext, \wtexttext) = \text{\dfrac{}{\tile{i=1}{n}}\tile{j=1}{n}}\probsin(i, j, w)\). Here, \(p\) is a multinomial distribution with parameters \(\pi\) and \(\personal_pamphletimber\) for each word \(w\) and each token \(i\), \(j\), and \(n\), respectively.

4. **Imitation Network**:
   - The implicit imitation is learned in two parts:
     1. **Learning Fine Control Signals**:
        - Learning a policy for fine control tasks that allows the agent to generate diverse outputs at various scales.
        - These signals are used to mimic experts' behavior when making their policies better yet to make the agent act like a static expert.
     2. **Imitation Loss**:
        - A linear inverse function \(I_{\theta} = \simple{postconnecitadelayer}(simplelarge(\pi,\postcode_wadland))\) is used to make it easier for expert and non-practitioner policies to learn how to reward each other.

Every candidate subscription word \(w\) is mimicked at a fixed log probability \(p(\postcode, \pretexttext|w)\), for each word \(w\) and each token \(i\).

5. **Integration**:
   - The model integrates knowledge about state prediction (via \(p(\postcode_, \pretexttext|w), p(\postcode_, \pretexttexttheta_w\) and policy for each \(w\) and token \(i\) are also learned.
   - LDC sends (in log prob logit form) large and small states \(w\) that are trained to become fast, high-level, and invariant.
   - Experience with these good embeddings is cemented via Non negative reweighting.
   - LDC receives non-deterministic policy gradients, which direct policy with respect to the hidden states.
   - All parameters for state prediction and one hidden layer network are learned together through the LDC.
   - The \(\postcode\) and transition probabilities between states are compared and smoothed.
   - The LDC takes the input images, generates a common representation of the input image, uses this common rep \(\space(\proidescribes p(\postcode,\) and the social hierarchy, and asks \(\\)_is the next letter sent from \(w\).

6. **Technical Challenges**:
   - The model needs significant fine-tuning, since non-reproducible noise \(\phonescript_{\randomwo}\), multiple inputs.
   - The model does not generalize well across agents.
   - The rich representation of state and environment trajectories makes it difficult to align and coordinate.
   - The directional aspects of the relationship often bias predictions towards disfavored subtopics at higher hierarchical levels.
   - There can be more than one top-state, making it difficult to learn interpretable representations of state and environment trajectories.
   - While the model takes rewards into account for state prediction, the advantage of the policy-related context remains tuned out. Knowledge of sign and magnitude does not seem to appear early in training.

### Page 16

ignoring future inflation, we assume that initially \( W_{0} = 0 \) and \( W_{1} = 1 \) . Our goal will be to show that the model's predictions alone will not adequately explain the spread between \( r \) and \( w \) at different initial conditions \( x_{0} \) .

To understand the model's behavior, we start by examining the underlying function and its behaviors. Given the friction matrix \( F \) , the model can be written as \( \mathbf{w}=e^{-t}(\sigma(\mathbf{w}_{t})) \) . The first term in this equation can be interpreted as the exponential decay of \( w \) over time. Given parameters selected by \( \mathbf{w}_{0} \) and \( \mathbf{w}_{1} \) , \( \sigma(\mathbf{w}_{t}) = e^{-t\sigma(\mathbf{w}_{0})} \) . The parameters \( \sigma \) and \( \sigma_{0} \) are bound between 0 and 1, leading to the values \( \sigma(0) = \sigma_{0} \) and \( \sigma(1) = \sigma_{1} \) . Given \( \sigma_{0} \) , the model will converge after a large number of steps.

The paper also discusses the impact of the start conditions \( x_{0} \) and \( x_{1} \) . If the stochastic noise introduces variability at the beginning, the model's predictions may not be accurate. If the noise increases as the hole fills rather than at the point of least resistance, the model's predictions may also be suboptimal.

To showcase the model's predictions in a simple example, Figure 10 shows the convergence to a narrow range for \( x_{0} \in \{0.1, 0.5\} \) and \( x_{1} = 0 \) (top), and closing and opening for \( x_{0} \in [0, 0.1]0.5] \) at various horizons (bottom). The difference in predictions over time is due to the initial random variable \( x_{1} \) .

To illustrate the model's convergence, the paper generates a series of \( W_{1} \) that outline the picture of the SPSA, starting from the SPSA, SPSA-HERM, Hyper-Bernoulli-HERM, and Bernoulli Hamiltonian HESRMR. The SPSA and SPSA-HERM subsets demonstrate that the model finds both of the steady states where the strike price \( W_{0} \) and ratio between the expected risk and expected return are close to 1.

To demonstrate the costs of using random-walk conductances, the paper analyses the results of a simple model to select markets and quantities of S&P500 Holdings and Microsoft using random-walk conductances. The model's predictions are inaccurate, and random walks for both of the markets and scenarios yield better results.

To further demonstrate the phenomenon, the paper analyzes the dynamics of S&P500 Holdings dataset, using SILAB model rand_t plot to show in what zones S&P500 Holdings is ex-ante likely to end the day. The model's predictions are accurate in the upper half of the plot, but make predictions just above or below the line for short term predictions. Similarly, analysis of the monthly movement of the EURO STOXX 50 index yields similar results.

## 4.1. Alternatives

The paper examines alternative ways of forming the final data point where the strike price \( W_{0} \) hits the central range of 1. This alternative investigation does not account for the effects of stochasticity between time intervals of the interest-rate horizon.
